name: Zeigarnik Effect
description: Interrupted or unfinished tasks tend to stay mentally active and keep pulling for closure. In design practice this is often framed as a memory effect, but the better-supported part is the urge to resume and complete the open task.
design_relevance_note: Shows up in progress indicators, saved-draft flows, cliffhanger onboarding, and 'continue where you left off' patterns that rely on unfinished work staying cognitively active.
myth_risk_note: The popular 'interrupted tasks are remembered better' framing is itself the myth-risk-bearing part -- already documented in this entry's own review_note as disputed by a real meta-analysis -- while the underlying resumption-tendency effect is genuinely backed. Rated low, not high, because real peer-reviewed backing already exists in the corpus; this pass's own empty result reflects an alias-query problem, not a literature gap.
prevalence_note: Common in behavioral-design, onboarding, and copywriting discussions under the 'open loops' framing, but less universal in mainstream UX canon than Fitts's, Hick's, or Jakob's Law.

findings.description: A meta-analysis aggregating modern studies found no reliable overall memory advantage for interrupted/unfinished tasks over completed ones once replication attempts are combined — directly complicating the popular 'Zeigarnik effect' memory-boost framing used in design practice.
findings.source_title: Interruption, Recall and Resumption: A Meta-Analysis of the Zeigarnik and Ovsiankina Effects

findings.description: The same meta-analysis found a distinct, more robust effect: a genuine tendency for people to want to resume an interrupted task (the Ovsiankina effect) — open goals reliably intrude on attention and pull toward completion, even though this is not the same thing as a memory-encoding advantage. This is the part of the popular claim that actually survives scrutiny.
findings.source_title: Interruption, Recall and Resumption: A Meta-Analysis of the Zeigarnik and Ovsiankina Effects

applications.title: Duolingo's near-complete daily goal keeps users mid-lesson
applications.description: Growth.Design's UX teardown of Duolingo's onboarding and retention flow highlights a moment where a user is one lesson away from completing their daily goal and activating a streak -- the Zeigarnik Effect (people remember and are drawn back to uncompleted tasks more than completed ones) is named as the mechanism pulling the user to finish just one more lesson rather than stop.
applications.ethical_note: Nudging a genuinely motivated learner to finish one more lesson toward a self-chosen daily goal is a reasonable, largely user-beneficial use of the Zeigarnik Effect, but the same mechanism -- exploiting the discomfort of an unfinished task -- is also the engine behind streak-driven engagement pressure that this corpus's own Duolingo-adjacent entries have flagged as a source of user frustration when a streak breaks, so it is graded mixed rather than a clean user_beneficial.
